{"docket_number": "25", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1966", "first_party": "United States", "first_party_label": "Appellant", "second_party": "Arnold Schwinn & Co., Schwinn Cycle Distributors Association", "second_party_label": "Appellee", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Appeal", "lower_court": null, "argued": ["1967-04-20T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Does Schwinn’s practice of only selling products to approved dealers violated the Sherman Act?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

The United States brought an antitrust action against Arnold, Schwinn & Co. and its distributor Schwinn Cycle Distributors Association. Arnold only allowed distributors to sell its products to approved dealers. The United States complaint attached this practice as an unlawful restraint on trade. The district court held that this practice was unlawful as to sales from distributors to dealers, but allowed for sales directly from Arnold to dealers. The Supreme Court heard this case on direct appeal

", "conclusion": "

Sometimes. In a 5-2 decision, Justice Abe Fortas wrote the majority opinion reversing the lower court. The Supreme Court held that it is unreasonable for a manufacturer to restrict where its products are sold after it has transferred title and responsibility for loss. In situations where Arnold retains title, and the dealer acts as an agent or salesperson, those restrictions are not a restraint on trade. Justice Potter Stewart wrote a partial dissent, expressing disagreement with the majority’s argument that Arnold’s practices become illegal when carried out through a distributor. Justice John M. Harlan joined in the partial dissent. Justice Tom C. Clark and Justice Byron R. White did not participate.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 25, United States Appellant v. Arnold Schwinn and Company. Mr. Pazzer. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This, like the preceding case, is here on direct appeal by the government under the Expediting Act. And like the preceding case, it involves a charge of restrictive practices in the marketing of a branded product in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. In the present case, however, the restraint is not one imposed on licensed manufacturers by a trademark licensor whom they control, but one imposed by a single manufacturer upon his chain of distribution, upon the distributors and dealers, the wholesalers and retailers who carry his product. The manufacturer here, Schwinn, asserts the right to designate, or in its terms franchise, the independent retail outlets that shall carry its goods. And also, and this is what we challenge, to prevent any retailer not specifically approved by it, not franchised, from selling its products. The government's complaint was filed in 1958 and named three defendants. The first, of course, is Arnold Schwinn and Company, a family corporation engaged almost exclusively in the manufacture of bicycles and bicycle parts and accessories. The second defendant was the second defendant was the Schwinn Cycle Distributors Association, an association of some 20-odd wholesalers specializing in the distribution of bicycles. And the members of this association, the wholesalers who compose it, are the primary channel through which Schwinn distributes its products to the retail level. Now, the third defendant was the B.F. Goodrich Company, which primarily, of course, is a manufacturer of rubber goods, but which also distributes Schwinn bicycles both at wholesale to Goodrich's own franchised, independent franchise dealers, and at retail through a number of stores that Goodrich itself owns. Now, Goodrich is no longer in the case, having entered into a consent decree with the government before trial. I should mention here that Schwinn did not sell directly to the 5,000-odd independent retailers whom it franchised. They bought either from members of the Distributors Association or from other wholesalers. Now, it's true that Schwinn often shipped directly to the franchisees at paying a commission, as it was termed, to the wholesalers. This was the Schwinn plan. For reasons explained in our brief, we view these two as sales by the wholesalers. This is an issue, however, which has only to do with the scope of any decree entered here and doesn't involve the legality of the basic restraint. Now, the complaint charged that, beginning in 1952, the defendants conspired among themselves and with Schwinn distributors and franchise dealers to fix the franchise dealers' retail prices, to assign exclusive sales territories to the distributors, the wholesalers, and to prevent non-franchise dealers from getting hold of or selling Schwinn products by means of a concerted refusal of these conspirators to deal with any such non-franchised outlet. A trial on these charges was held in 1962 and 1963 before Judge Perry in the Northern District of Illinois, and it lasted 70 days. I mention the length of the trial advisedly to underscore the fact that, at defendants' insistence, the fullest possible record exploring the background and asserted justifications of the challenged practices was made, and there can be no contention that the defendants were prevented from introducing any evidence that they deemed relevant. Did you say 70 days? 70 days, yes. At the conclusion of the trial, the court delivered its opinion in January 1965, and it enjoined the territorial restraint, and defendants had not appealed from that injunction. And the court dismissed the other charges. Now, since we did not appeal from the dismissal of the retail price-fixing charge, the charge that the franchisees' prices were fixed by Schwinn, the only issue before the court is the concerted refusal by Schwinn distributors and dealers and Schwinn and the association to deal with any non-franchised outlet. A constraint, a concerted refusal, which has two aspects. The first being a prohibition by Schwinn against its distributors selling to any non-franchised outlet, and the second and complementary prohibition against the franchisees selling to any non-franchised outlet, the practice known as bootlegging. And we've called this double-faceted restraint an outlet limitation because its effect is to give Schwinn absolute control over what retail outlets shall carry its products. Disapproved outlets are frozen out since they are forbidden, since they cannot buy, may not buy, from either Schwinn distributors or Schwinn franchisees. Now, the first question, and considering the legality of this restraint, of course, is whether it was affected by concerted action. Because if this outlet limitation is a purely unilateral measure of Schwinn's, it is beyond the reach of Section 1. The District Court made no finding on this point. Of course, his view was that the limitation was, in any event, a reasonable restraint. But we think it abundantly clear from the record that Schwinn, by threats and persuasion and cajolery and policing, did join with its distributors and dealers in a concerted refusal to deal. And the evidence on which we rely is discussed at some length in our opening and reply brief. And since no issue of general significance is involved, I prefer not to burden the argument with it, except to say this, that Schwinn itself concedes in its brief, page 34, that it, in its words, requested its distributors to limit shipments to franchise dealers. And generally, that request was followed. Elsewhere in the brief, it speaks of using request and persuasion to gain the distributor's adherence to this plan. And we think that under Park Davis, Schwinn plainly went beyond a simple announcement of policy and engaged in the requisite concerted action for a Sherman Act violation. Now, I could perhaps stop here and invoke the principle that boycotts are forbidden by the antitrust laws in any and all circumstances, because what the facts show is precisely a boycott by Schwinn and its distributors and dealers of outlets which did not receive the Schwinn imprimatur. We don't, however, rely on that rule, and this for two reasons. First, we know of no cases involving application of the rule in which there were not significant elements of a horizontal restraint, of competitors ganging up against the excluded tradesmen. Here we grant, in contrast to the Seeley case, that the initiative in this applet limitation was Schwinn's and that the limitation may appropriately be viewed as a genuinely vertical one. And, of course, the antitrust laws have generally treated vertical restraints somewhat more leniently than horizontal. Now, secondly, whatever label one attaches to this kind of concerted refusal, which is certainly a form of boycott, we're not prepared to assert that it is so invariably pernicious and unjustifiable as to warrant a blanket rule of condemnation. And when I come to discuss the circumstances of Schwinn's outlet limitation, I shall suggest, by way of contrast, some situations where we think that such a concerted refusal should perhaps be tolerated because they actually advance important antitrust objectives. Now, so saying, I don't mean to suggest that we don't propose a quite strict standard of legality, of illegality for vertical restraints of this character because, plainly, concerted efforts to enforce a restricted as opposed to a competitive distribution system go against the antitrust grain and are highly suspect. And we would say that when the plaintiff has established that such a restraint significantly impairs competition in the distribution of the manufacturer's product, it is prima facie bad. The burden at that point is on the defendant to justify it, and we think it's a heavy burden. I'm not sure I understand the distinction that you're drawing between your position here and the government's position in sealing. Now, if you assume that here you have not only a vertical restraint, but also what you were referring to as concerted action, aren't you saying that here you have a horizontal as well as a vertical restraint? I think not. I think the distinction we would draw would be in terms of the initiative. In the General Motors case of last terms, the boycott of bootleg dealers originated on the dealer level. Dealers got together and petitioned General Motors to stop this practice. And in Seeley, we regard that as a situation where a group of competitors get together and restrict competition between them. I'm not sure that I don't believe I got that impression. Seeley, if you're talking about the calendar and the chronology, I don't recall that that was the situation in Seeley. Are you talking about the chronology? That is to say, where did the impulse for the restraint come from in the first instance? Not as a matter of time, but when competitors join together in eliminating competition, and there is no third party here, a manufacturer, who has an interest not in restricting competition as such between his distributors, but in advancing some further end, there is a greater possibility of justification. But I'd prefer not to... I may be missing your point. I think this is crucial to a decision in these two cases, so far as I'm concerned, because I thought that the presentation in Seeley was to the effect that, regardless of chronology or who started this, that there were meetings and there were decisions made in which the licensees participated with Seeley. And Seeley has some characteristics that are given a purpose and a being of its own, but nevertheless, I thought the argument was, the licensees got together with Seeley and participated in these territorial restrictions. The government claims existed, and therefore the government says it's a Percy violation. Now here, as I understand it, you're saying that this was... these territorial restraints were... or the restraints on outlets were originated by Schwinn, but you're saying that there was a concert among the distributors, and this is not Percy. Maybe I'm wrong, and maybe mature thought will change my mind about this, but at the moment I confess that it seems to me to be twiddled in, twiddled in. Well, I'd rather not argue the Seeley case, but if Seeley has indeed a life of its own, with regard to the territorial limitations in Seeley, not the other functions which the Seeley entity performs, but with respect to dividing territories, if it indeed has a life of its own, as White Motor had a life apart from that of its distributors, then perhaps the two cases are similar. I think Mr. Friedman may have gone, he may have heart failure in his... I'd like to turn to the Genesis, and the... Some of the... That's true. That's definitely true. Yes. In discussing this limitation, I would start with 1952, the first year mentioned in the complaint in the year that restrictive distribution was adopted by Schwinn. Now, that year, Schwinn made and sold some 500,000 bicycles, and that was almost 20% of the total bicycle sales in the United States, including imports. Schwinn being one of a small group of manufacturers who dominated and still dominate the bicycle industry. Not only was Schwinn the nation's leading bicycle manufacturer, but it had... Its sales had grown greatly over the years, faster than the industries as a whole, and in 1952, we're at their... We're near their peak. The reason for this growth, so far as one can reconstruct it from the record, appears to be that Schwinn had pioneered a number of technical innovations in bicycle manufacture and had earned a reputation for high quality. And it had done so, and had reached the top of its industry without finding it necessary or appropriate to regiment its distribution, because until 1952, Schwinn made no effort whatsoever to limit the dealers to whom its distributors resold or otherwise to regulate the price or other terms of retail sale of Schwinn's. Now, despite the company's success with this open marketing policy, which had brought them to the summit of the industry, some Schwinn officials were dissatisfied with their distribution setup, their concern being basically that with Schwinn bicycles so widely available to the public and so many retail outlets, dealers had no particular incentive to advertise and promote Schwinn over other brands, and they might even trade on Schwinn's reputation for high quality by using Schwinn as a... by granting large discounts on Schwinn in order to perhaps sell cheaper merchandise to the... or other merchandise to the public. And in a word, these officials felt that the company's open marketing policy was not calculated to develop a loyal and devoted dealer network. And there's much talk in the record and in Schwinn's brief of loyalty. A restricted distribution was adopted to remedy this problem, first by giving Schwinn dealers sufficient protection or security, franchising for security being a favorite Schwinn phrase, security against competition in the retail sale of Schwinn's so that it would profit them to concentrate on that line. And secondly, by excluding from its chain of distribution discount houses and price cutters because those outlets would undermine the security, the profits, and the loyalty of Schwinn dealers and might also, and significantly, damage Schwinn's high price, Schwinn's premium image as the premium domestic bicycle. This design was implemented in several steps. The first was to recruit retailers who Schwinn felt had the potential of loyal and effective dealers. Schwinn's wholesalers were asked to distribute franchise applications to their dealer accounts to be filled in and returned to Schwinn for its approval. And when the application was approved, a franchise contract was issued between the dealer and Schwinn. Now this contract contains, on the dealer's side, promises to advertise and promote the Schwinn line and to give Schwinn equal representation with other lines sold by the retailer. And in exchange, Schwinn promises to furnish certain advertising and promotional aids. And also, and this is crucial, Schwinn promises to, I quote, offer the dealer a market with an established potential and a limited number of authorized Schwinn dealers. In other words, Schwinn promised not to so saturate the market with franchise outlets as to dilute the value of the franchise. And to fulfill this covenant against dilution, Schwinn refused to franchise dealers in areas where, franchise additional dealers in areas where it felt it already had adequate representation. And beyond that, while the company seems to have had few affirmative criteria for franchising, it franchised all kinds of outlets, toy stores, hardware stores, department stores, stores that offered no service at all as well as those that had repair shops. It was consistent in refusing to franchise a discount house or a known price cutter. And this was a policy, this refusal to accept known price cutters, that served three important objectives relating to this general purpose of security and protection for the franchisee. first, it protected them from price competition, which might erode their loyalty to Schwinn by reducing their profits on the sale of Schwinn. Secondly, after Schwinn in 1952 adopted resale price maintenance through enforcement of state fair trade statutes, refusing to accept applications from price cutters served to avoid the difficult judicial enforcement problems that fair trade involves. And thirdly, this policy protected the Schwinn name from association with discount merchandising, an association that concerned Schwinn greatly. Now, had Schwinn gone no further than this in trying to bind its dealers to it, we probably would not be here. Our concern is with the additional steps that Schwinn took to make the franchise a greater assurance of protection and profit for the franchisees. That is, its action in joining with its distributors and franchise dealers to prevent any retailer denied a franchise from getting his hands on Schwinn, the result being to give the Schwinn franchisees as a group a monopoly in the sale of the brand. Now, we begin in analyzing the reasonableness of a restraint of this sort, a concerted refusal to deal with unauthorized outlets by observing that in the circumstances of this case, this restraint impairs competition in a deliberate and substantial fashion, and not merely incidentally or trivially. Schwinn avowedly desired to protect its franchisees from what it regarded as too much competition so that they would have a large enough profit in selling Schwinn's to give them an incentive to push this line over competing brands. This was the core of Schwinn's conception of effective distribution. protection. In order to make this protection effective, it was important to prevent the product from leaking out, as it were, to any non-franchised retailers, especially if they were price cutters or discount houses. These additional outlets would have crowded the franchisees, especially if they cut prices, would have made the Schwinn line less attractive to the franchisees because less profitable to them. And so this isn't a case where elimination of competition is a byproduct of a transaction with another purpose. A merger between competitors always eliminates competition, but its motivation or purpose may be nothing more than to solve a management problem. And this isn't a case where a manufacturer excludes certain retail outlets, not because he wants to curtail competition, but because he wants to protect some legitimate goodwill. For example, by keeping his brands out of the hands of a disreputable merchant, a merchant who uses misrepresentation, something of that sort, Schwinn's outlet limitation wasn't aimed at disreputable or dishonest or incompetent dealers. It wasn't an effort to enforce reasonable standards of sales or service or appearance or showroom or what have you on its dealers. It was, and I stress again, it avowedly was a device for protecting the franchisees from too much, from what Schwinn regarded as too much competition, especially price competition from discount houses and other known price cutters. And I don't think I need labor the point that a practice which by its very design substantially lessens competition distribution is highly suspect under antitrust law. And in truth, this outlet limitation is quite similar to a resale price maintenance agreement, which, except as sheltered by the Maguire Act, is of course illegal in all circumstances. And I think it's no accident to observe in this connection that Schwinn did have a fair trade program operated in conjunction with this outlet limitation. In both kinds of restraint, what the manufacturer is trying to do is to offer his dealers protection from competition in the retail sale of his brand in the hope that that will induce him to push this brand over other brands, other brands as to which retailer may not have a substantial profit margin because there's very intense intra-brand competition. Mr. Posner, I'd like to ask you a few questions and see if I can refine in my own mind just what the government's position is. Now, I suppose that if Schwinn had dealt directly with retailers and had selected certain retailers and not others and had franchised certain retailers and not others, that the government would not be, would not consider that a violation of their trust standing alone. Is that right? That's true. Now, I suppose that the government that Schwinn could select certain distributors similarly and sell to them and not to other distributors. Could the, could Schwinn sell to certain distributors, sell to distributors, transfer title to them, and on condition that they should sell only to designated, retailers designated unilaterally by Schwinn and not by others. Well, that is one half of the restraint we're challenging here. That's something that you're reaching here. So that even if these, even if these retailers, the franchise retailers, were selected by Schwinn and by Schwinn alone without any participation by the distributors, the government would challenge that. And you say that there was participation here in the sense that distributors participated in policing this franchise arrangement, not otherwise. Is that so? Correct. Yes. I'm not suggesting that the distributors chose, they participated in the process. Now, one of the things that bothers me in your statement of the case, your very opening, is that you dismissed the so-called Schwinn plan. And under the Schwinn plan, the court below, as I remember, found that Schwinn sold to the retailer. In other words, that it was a direct sale by Schwinn to the retailer. Is that correct? Correct. Now, you say that Schwinn did pay a commission or something of the sort to the distributor in those transactions. But you say that the government does not accept that, and that you think it's wrong, it's a conclusion of law, and that it's wrong, I suppose. Correct. And that those have to be treated as sales by Schwinn to the distributor. That's correct. The reason I passed it over lightly is that we're entitled to a decree, even if the court agrees that Schwinn plans sales are direct to the retailer, for two reasons. First, because unquestionably, Schwinn made many sales to wholesalers, who then resold to its retailers. And secondly, because the bootlegging facet of the restraint would not be affected. General Motors sold directly to its dealers, but nevertheless, we argued last term that it could not prevent them from reselling to bootleg to other outlets. So here, even if Schwinn sells directly to retailers, we don't think it is permissible for it to forbid those retailers to sell to other outlets. Well, we have tried to be a little precise about these things in a way, in our own analysis of the problem, so I think I may be wrong, but I do think that it's kind of important to get this specifically. The sales under the Schwinn plan, I've forgotten, were they quite substantial? A substantial percentage? Yes, they were about 50% of them. Of Schwinn's total sales? Of Schwinn's total sales, yes. And now, what about the consignment sales? That's another category. They are very, very insignificant, and the Schwinn in its brief says that since the trial, it doesn't use consignment. There were also some formal agency agreements, which I think are either de minimis in terms of volume or have been discontinued. But does the government take the position that regardless of the transfer of title and transfer of ownership under the various methods of distribution, that the economic and legal effect for any trust purposes is the same under all of the methods of distribution? In the circumstances of this case, yes. could I ask you a question for you, Mr. Posner? Why is it that the government doesn't feel this case is controlled by General Motors? Because in General Motors, what happened was that the franchise dealers in Los Angeles got together and decided to stamp out this bootlegging, and they went to a relatively passive General Motors and prodded General Motors into using its power to make effective their attempts to... But after that, they were all in the same boat, General Motors and the dealers. Correct. And here, they end up in the same boat, too. They end up in the same boat. Perhaps I could illustrate by means of an example. You see, what we are concerned with is a rule that would forbid limiting athletes in all circumstances. And that would be the... That is the problem. As an example, I would suggest that of the new entrant in an industry like the automobile industry where a retail dealer must make a large investment in showroom and parts and inventory and sales personnel in order to carry the brand. And the dealer may not be willing to carry an unknown brand in those circumstances without some initial protection from competition. And because the antitrust laws do want to encourage entry into concentrated industries, that having been observed just last week in the Clorox opinion, we suggest that the court leave open the possibility of an initial outlet limitation designed to encourage a retailer to carry a new brand, although we also think that would have to be a restraint limited as to duration, just long enough to enable the retailer to recoup his heavy initial costs. Now... But you don't say then in this case that it's a per se rule at all? No. It's not... But the only difference with the per se rule is you make out your case just by showing the restriction, but it's subject to rebuttal? Yes. We would go a little beyond showing the... not just showing the existence of the contract. We will... We assume the burden of showing that intra-brand competition is substantially affected adversely. At that point, we leave it open to the defendant to come in and show that this restraint is justified. But the general motors, you wouldn't have to do that, would you? No. General... No. We would just show the outlet limitation and stop. Yes. I have just suggested one instance where we think an outlet limitation would be reasonable. And let me now say why we think the limitation is not reasonable as practiced by Schwinn. Point out that no large investment is required for a bicycle dealer to handle a new brand. That no bicycle manufacturer other than Schwinn has found it necessary to restrict competition in distribution in order to get effective distribution. And I point out too that when Schwinn embarked on restricted distribution, it was not a new entrant. It was one of the best established seller of bicycles with the largest market share in the industry, a share of 20%, and it had achieved this pinnacle of consumer acceptance without limiting competition and distribution, despite the fact that Schwinn's are a higher priced brand. Now, it's true, of course, that Schwinn felt it could entrench this consumer acceptance for the brand still more deeply by giving its dealers added incentive to push the Schwinn line through this drastic limitation of intra-brand competition. But this is not, in our view, any justification. The consuming public, we think, is entitled, under antitrust principles, to the benefits which may be considerable. In the competition, in the distribution of so important a brand as Schwinn, a brand that accounts for 20% of all bicycles sold in this country, the costs of distributing Schwinn might be lower, and the price to the consumer might be lower if there were a diversity of outlets handling this product, if there were price competition, as well as aggressive promotion by this selected group of dealers. And this interest, in our view, may not outweigh perhaps the interest in having a new company come into a concentrated industry and stir up some new competition, but it does outweigh the interest of an established and large and prosperous manufacturer, the number one firm in its industry, in growing still larger. And even if we assume, as Schwinn argues, that this kind of restricted competition increases inter-brand competition in the sense that it makes Schwinn a stronger competitor, we wouldn't regard this as justification, because we would ask, how is the consumer, for whose benefit the antitrust laws are chiefly designed, how is he benefited by more aggressive promotion of Schwinn bicycles by retailers who have this financial stake based on protection from competition in pushing the Schwinn line over other brands? The consumer might be a lot better off with a disinterested dealer who would recommend bicycle brands to him on the merits rather than on the benefit of which manufacturer. It gives him the most protection against intra-brand competition. And there's a further point. To the extent that restricted distribution may have helped Schwinn, I might interrupt to say that the record actually suggests it may have hurt Schwinn, whose market share and sales had declined after it adopted this system. But be that as it may, assuming it did strengthen Schwinn, we think it may actually have impaired rather than enhanced the strength of competition in this industry. The purpose of this output limitation is to substitute advertising and promotional and intense sales effort for price as a method of competition. competition. This, of course, is what economists call product differentiation, competing by stressing the real or imagined differences between your brand and competing brands of the same product. And this court has noted just the other day in the Clorox opinion the effects which product differentiation may have on the health of a concentrated industry. because where you have manufacturers who create a consumer allegiance to their particular brands, a consumer loyalty based on aggressive promotion, it is the more difficult for a new firm to rest a share of the market away from the established firms, and so the threat of entry is diminished. Schwinn here is asking the court's indulgence of the clogs which it places on competition and distribution precisely to enable it the more effectively to differentiate its brand from other brands in the consumer's mind by this aggressive sales efforts, and this in an industry which is highly concentrated, where in 1961 the four largest firms, Schwinn then being number two, had as a group 49% of the nation's bicycle sales, including imports. Now while we don't argue that the output limitation is bad because it may harm the prospects for new entry in an industry like this, we certainly think it's no excuse, no justification for the patent effects which the limitation has on intra-brand competition. And let me close with just a brief word on the suggestion that we are here advocating a rule that bears harshly on small business or on the institution of franchising. I point out first that by the standards of the bicycle industry, which are the only standards relevant here, Schwinn is not a small but a large company, and we recognize exceptions to this rule. Again, we're not advocating a per se rule. We recognize exceptions in cases where the franchisor is a new entrant or perhaps, as in the Packard case, a weak or fading firm or a small company. Moreover, the rule we're arguing for is not one limited to firms which are too small to do their own wholesaling. As I pointed out in a colloquy with Mr. Justice Fortas, one of the restraints here challenged is identical to that that was an issue in the General Motors case, that of preventing your retailers from selling to other outlets. And finally, while the Schwinn program may have increased the profits of those Schwinn, of the dealers who were fortunate enough to obtain and retain franchises, thousands of dealers were either refused franchises or had their franchises terminated. And by virtue of this outlet limitation, this concerted refusal to deal, they were thereby completely frozen out of the distribution of Schwinn. And these small businessmen were hurt and not helped by the challenge restraint. Now, finally, as to... But that's the small businessman argument, isn't it? You don't look at the franchisor, I wish you look at the franchisee. That's the argument, isn't it? The highways of America are aligned with motels and frozen custard emporia and a variety of other more or less unattractive phenomena, which represent, in the 1960s, the opportunity for the ma and pa operation in America. You get a franchise from anything as, from such a thing as big as quality court to something as small as a little ice cream cone stand with a franchise and a trademark. Nothing, we say, touches in the slightest the examples you've given, which are examples of business franchising and are the kind of thing that, to our knowledge, represents the trend in franchising. That is, when a Howard Johnson's chain or Quality Courts or Corvell or Holiday Inn go about setting up new businesses, helping small businessmen to get into business, not to sell a product by limiting distribution, but to create a uniform, recognizable name through this league of small businessmen. None of the problems of this case arise. None of the... I would be sure, without knowing, that an essential part of such a franchise would be exclusive territoriality. It would not be. It is possible that Holiday Inn might promise not to franchise another Holiday Inn in the immediate area or... But that's not the kind of thing where... That would be a necessary part of the deal, I should think, before... It might be, but that's not... Before a couple would put their life savings into something, they would want to know that the same thing wouldn't open up across the street. That's true, and that is not the kind of thing we're concerned with. We're not asking Schwinn to franchise anybody that it doesn't want or to promise, or we're not saying that Schwinn can't promise not to limit its authorized outlets. We're concerned when the safety valve, which such phenomena as bootlegging represent, is closed off completely where the non-authorized outlet has no chance to sell these goods in competition with the franchisees. I would suggest some other distinctions between Schwinn's franchise program and other franchise programs to suggest how narrow is the rule we're contending for here. First of all, Schwinn's franchise program is validly aimed at price cutters and discount houses, and one hopes that this kind of objective is not typical of franchising programs. Is not what? Is not typical of franchising programs. That they're directed against discounting.
